What is irritating to the eyes are chloramines, chlorine bonded with nitrogen. Urine, dirt, leaves, and grass are all sources. Chloramines still kill germs, but they are irritating. You need to shock them out of the water by bumping the chlorine very high.

As long as the pH levels are good, you can have a high level of chlorine without irritation. When the water is a bit cloudy and smells really "chloriney," then you know that the chloramines are high and will be irritating.

This concludes my pool operator training skills.

This is hardly breaking news, folks. Learned all this in a swimming pool operations class in the early 1980s.

You normally keep the pool at 1.5 PPM of chlorine. As the free chlorine bonds with any source of nitrogen (nitrogenous wastes), it forms chloramines. Chloramines are what you typically associate with the strong smell of chlorine at a pool; as the chloramines start to build up, the water becomes a bit cloudy and has a strong chlorine odor even though the total PPM is still around 1.5. This is when it irritates your eyes.

To eliminate the chloramines, you hyperchlorinate, raising the chlorine level to 4.5 - 6 PPM. This shocks the chloramines out of the pool.

The issue is that you need to keep the pH level in check when the chlorine is that high, or it will be irritating. If you maintain the pH in the ideal range (7.2 - 7.4), 4.5-6 PPM of chlorine is not at all irritating.

The reason pool operators don't shock the chloramines out of the system all the time is that the pH has probably gone too high to correct. You can lower it a bit with muriatic acid, but as calcium is leached out of the pool walls, it will eventually create a buffered solution, forcing the pH to become more basic and preventing it from dropping. At this point, you need to drain some water and start fresh.

So all pool managers are aware of this, and they don't care that the pool is irritating because chloramines still kill germs. Plus, they have learned to dislike kids.

That wasn't in the class, but:

http://chlorine.chemicalassociation.com/Chlorine-Benefits/Safe-Water/Pool-Treatment-101.html

Shock treatment adds a larger than normal amount of oxidizing chemicals to pool water. This additional dose destroys organic contaminants and oxidizes ammonia and nitrogen compounds to rid the area of irritating chloramine odor and, if chlorine is used for the purpose, to sanitize the water.

The software contributed to the issue. With no internal angle of attack indicator and no visibility, the pilots were confused when the stall warnings stopped.

In an article in a prominent magazine, a noted aviation expert observed that once the angle of attack was so extreme, the system rejected the data as invalid and temporarily stopped the stall warnings. However, "this led to a perverse reversal that lasted nearly to the impact: each time the pilot happened to lower the nose, rendering the angle of attack marginally less severe, the stall warning sounded again—a negative reinforcement that may have locked him into his pattern of pitching up," which increased the angle of attack and thus prevented the aircraft from recovering from its stall.

The problem is that in the four minutes after the autopilot disengaged, they apparently never realized that they were stalled because they had no reliable gauge of airspeed. The stall alarm turned off when the nose was raised at an extreme angle because of the impossible instrument readings, and restarted when they lowered the nose. The engines were at full load throughout.

It looks like the first officer mismanaged the situation by keeping the nose up, while the captain probably never realized the control was still pulled back as his were not, since the controls are not linked. All they knew was that the altitude indicator was dropping, but since the airspeed indicators were wildly fluctuating and the stall alarm seemed random, they likely faced the situation very confused.

All in all, not a great example of poor piloting; the software seems to have been inadequate.

Fly-by-wire issues. It is likely that the pilots didn't realize that the controls would allow them to make inputs that could lead to a stall, as they typically wouldn't. However, if the failsafes were functioning, the autopilot wouldn't have disengaged.

The disconnected controls, the absence of a clear indicator that informs pilots of the aircraft's mode at all times, and most importantly, a visible angle of attack indicator were the key issues that needed addressing after the investigation into the flight data recorder. The initial problem was the airspeed sensors freezing, which resulted in unreliable airspeed readings, causing the autopilot to disengage. These sensors had been flagged for replacement prior to the incident.

The exact sequence of events remains unclear. When the captain returned from a break, the aircraft was at a significant pitch and at cruising altitude. He attempted to lower the nose, but this triggered the stall alert, leading to the assumption that the copilot kept pulling back to silence the alarm.

It is quite alarming to think about waking from a break and finding oneself in the pilot's seat with a distressed copilot, an intermittent stall warning, no visual references, airspeed readings fluctuating wildly, and as you secure your seatbelt, the altitude begins to drop rapidly.

The main critique is that they did not conduct a thorough check of all indicators and controls as a team. It is likely that the captain would have realized that the aircraft's attitude was due to the copilot's inputs and would have adjusted the nose down to stabilize their altitude. The engines remained operational, so it seems that a more experienced pilot might have been able to disregard the stall warning and turbulence to assess when the wings were generating lift.

It all depends on what you land on.... There have been a good number of terminal velocity falls that were survived without a parachute. Generally, they involve crew members choosing to die from a fall rather than to burn to death on the way down. Through dumb luck (landing in a forest with branches, or on the side of a slope with deep snowfall, usually), they survive the 120 MPH landing.

A fall from 130 feet will have you moving at 50 MPH. If you land on stone or cement, you are toast. But people have landed on compressible dirt from this height (the best thing to land on, by the way; water is good, but the odds of getting knocked out by the shock and drowning are high) and NOT EVEN BEEN INJURED.

Car hoods, roofs, and soft dirt slow your deceleration significantly. People have been killed by the rebound onto a cement road.

So this is not at all impossible, especially if the pit was dirt at the bottom.

Because he wants to win. He was already the leader of this team in every way that counted, but at some level his personal at-bats reflected a bit of the kid going for glory. The only selfish thing about him as a player has been his desire for the big hit. At some deep level, he is a little kid that wants that glorious feeling of hitting a low fastball on the sweet spot of the bat, and it is indeed a glorious feeling, one of the most magical in sports, when you make that contact where the bat and the ball and your arms turn into a crazy yo-yo that launches the ball farther than seems possible. He wants it more than a big contract. He wants it more than the hall of fame. But I think putting him in the one spot has finally clicked that magic switch; the little kid wants to meet his responsibility as team leader more than he wants to be a hero, to hit that ball. And as we all knew, as he had to know at every level except the most important one deep in his brain muscle memory, by going deep into the count he still will get that chance to hit the ball, even if he lays off what could be a low fastball, but really is a slider headed for the plate. So the manager dumped an unfair load on his shoulders and he found his shoulders stronger than he thought.

Or, he is doing a zone hitting thing that pitchers figure out mid-July and it messes him up until late August. Either way, I love that kid; I am just hoping for the one that puts him in the hall of fame, because the statue at the stadium either has him blowing a bubble or I am putting it on myself.
